claim: Almost every neuropsychiatric condition shows sex and/or gender biases in risk, presentation, etiology, and prognosis.
source: Almost every neuropsychiatric condition shows sex and/or gender biases in risk, presentation, etiology, and prognosis (Green et al., 2019; Grissom and Reyes, 2019; Shansky, 2019).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature

claim: Sex-modulated biological mechanisms could modulate cognitive processes that confer vulnerability and/or resilience to mental health challenges.
source: This raises the possibility that sex-modulated biological mechanisms could modulate cognitive processes that confer vulnerability and/or resilience to mental health challenges.
evidence: Based on logical inference from the observation of sex biases in neuropsychiatric conditions

claim: Sex differences in cognitive task performance can be difficult to detect and even more variable than would be expected given the non-dichotomous, overlapping impacts of sex mechanisms on cognition.
source: However, sex differences in cognitive task performance can be difficult to detect and even more variable than would be expected given the non-dichotomous, overlapping impacts of sex mechanisms on cognition (Maney, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: There can be multiple ways to achieve the same level of performance on the primary dependent variables used to assess cognitive tasks.
source: An underrecognized source of variability in cognitive tasks is that there can be multiple ways to achieve the same level of performance on the primary dependent variables used to assess these tasks, such as 'number of correct responses'.
evidence: Based on established understanding of cognitive task performance

claim: Equivalent levels of performance could mask individual differences in how males and females are solving the same problem.
source: This means that equivalent levels of performance could mask individual differences in how males and females are solving the same problem.
evidence: Logical inference from the observation that multiple strategies can achieve the same performance

claim: Examining the latent strategies underlying task performance can reveal that individual males and females can take very different strategic paths to the learning of action-outcome associations.
source: Indeed, we have recently shown that examining the latent strategies underlying task performance --rather than differences in final performance--can reveal that individual males and females can take very different strategic paths to the learning of action-outcome associations (Chen et al., 2021b).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work by the authors

claim: Too little exploration makes behavior inflexible and perseverative.
source: Too little exploration makes behavior inflexible and perseverative.
evidence: Based on established understanding of exploration-exploitation tradeoff

claim: Too much exploration makes it impossible to sustain rewarding behaviors.
source: Too much makes it impossible to sustain rewarding behaviors.
evidence: Based on established understanding of exploration-exploitation tradeoff

claim: Exploration is dysregulated in numerous neuropsychiatric disorders.
source: Exploration is dysregulated in numerous neuropsychiatric disorders (Addicott et al., 2017; Wilson et al., 2021), many of which are also sex-biased (Green et al., 2019; Grissom and Reyes, 2019; Shansky, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Many neuropsychiatric disorders are sex-biased.
source: Exploration is dysregulated in numerous neuropsychiatric disorders (Addicott et al., 2017; Wilson et al., 2021), many of which are also sex-biased (Green et al., 2019; Grissom and Reyes, 2019; Shansky, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Sex differences in exploration and exploitation could contribute to sex-linked vulnerability to neuropsychiatric conditions.
source: This suggests that sex differences in exploration and exploitation could contribute to sex-linked vulnerability to these conditions, though we do not yet understand how exploration and exploitation differ with sex.
evidence: Logical inference from the observation that exploration is dysregulated in sex-biased disorders

claim: Exploration is a major source of errors in task performance.
source: Because exploration is a major source of errors in task performance more broadly (Ebitz et al., 2019; Pisupati et al., 2019), sex-differences in exploration could contribute to performance differences and variability seen across tasks and speciess (Grissom and Reyes, 2019; van den Bos et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Sex-differences in exploration could contribute to performance differences and variability seen across tasks and species.
source: Because exploration is a major source of errors in task performance more broadly (Ebitz et al., 2019; Pisupati et al., 2019), sex-differences in exploration could contribute to performance differences and variability seen across tasks and speciess (Grissom and Reyes, 2019; van den Bos et al., 2013).
evidence: Logical inference from the observation that exploration causes errors and is sex-different

claim: Male and female mice (n = 32, 16 per sex, strain B6129SF1/J) were trained to perform a restless two-armed spatial bandit task.
source: Age-matched male and female wild-type mice (n = 32, 16 per sex, strain B6129SF1/J, powered to detect differences in decision making Chen et al., 2021b) were trained to perform a restless two-armed spatial bandit task in touch-screen operant chambers (Figure 1A).
evidence: Direct description of experimental methods

claim: Males showed higher levels of exploration than females throughout the task.
source: Males showed higher levels of exploration than females throughout the task.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from the study

claim: Males were more likely to get 'stuck' in extended periods of exploration before committing to a favored choice.
source: This was because males were more likely to get 'stuck' in extended periods of exploration before committing to a favored choice.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from the study

claim: Females showed elevated reward learning specifically during bouts of exploration.
source: On the other hand, females showed elevated reward learning specifically during bouts of exploration, making exploratory trials more informative, which allowed them to start exploiting a favored choice earlier than males.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from the study

claim: Females' elevated reward learning during exploration allowed them to start exploiting a favored choice earlier than males.
source: On the other hand, females showed elevated reward learning specifically during bouts of exploration, making exploratory trials more informative, which allowed them to start exploiting a favored choice earlier than males.
evidence: Logical inference from the observation of elevated learning during exploration

claim: Sex exerts stronger influences on decision making during periods of learning and exploration than during stable choices.
source: Together, these results suggest that sex exerts stronger influences on decision making during periods of learning and exploration than during stable choices.
evidence: Inference from experimental data showing sex differences in exploration but not overall performance

claim: Exploration during decision making is altered in people diagnosed with addictions, depression, and neurodevelopmental disabilities.
source: Exploration during decision making is altered in people diagnosed with addictions, depression, and neurodevelopmental disabilities, pinpointing the neural mechanisms of exploration as a highly translational avenue for conferring sex-modulated vulnerability to neuropsychiatric diagnoses.
evidence: Based on established knowledge from clinical literature

claim: Each location in the restless two-armed bandit task offered some probability of reward, which changed slowly and randomly across trials, and independently across targets.
source: Each location offered some probability of reward, which changed slowly and randomly across trials, and independently across targets.
evidence: Direct description of experimental methods

claim: Mice performed two repetitions of four consecutive sessions of the restless bandit task, measuring eight sessions in total.
source: Mice performed two repetitions of four consecutive sessions of the restless bandit task, measuring eight sessions in total.
evidence: Direct description of experimental methods

claim: Each session consisted of 300 trials.
source: Each session consisted of 300 trials.
evidence: Direct description of experimental methods

claim: There was no significant change in reward acquisition performance across sessions in both sexes.
source: There was no significant change in the reward acquisition performance across sessions in both sexes, demonstrating that both males and females have learned to perform the task and had reached an asymptotic level of performance (two-way repeated measure ANOVA, main effect of session, p = 0.71).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: Both males and females have learned to perform the task and had reached an asymptotic level of performance.
source: There was no significant change in the reward acquisition performance across sessions in both sexes, demonstrating that both males and females have learned to perform the task and had reached an asymptotic level of performance (two-way repeated measure ANOVA, main effect of session, p = 0.71).
evidence: Inference from the observation of stable performance across sessions

claim: There was no significant change in response time across sessions in both sexes.
source: There was no significant change in response time (two-way repeated measure ANOVA, main effect of session, p = 0.39) and reward retrieval time (main effect of session, p = 0.71) across sessions in both sexes, which again demonstrated that both sexes have learned how to perform the task.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: There was no significant change in reward retrieval time across sessions in both sexes.
source: There was no significant change in response time (two-way repeated measure ANOVA, main effect of session, p = 0.39) and reward retrieval time (main effect of session, p = 0.71) across sessions in both sexes, which again demonstrated that both sexes have learned how to perform the task.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: Mice were able to earn reward more frequently than chance regardless of sex.
source: Regardless of sex, mice were able to earn reward more frequently than chance (Figure 1B, two-way ANOVA, F(1, 60) = 228.9, p < 0.0001).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and shown in Figure 1B

claim: There was no significant sex difference in the probability of rewards acquired above chance.
source: There was no significant sex difference in the probability of rewards acquired above chance (Figure 1C, main effect of sex, F(1, 30) = 0.05, p = 0.83).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and shown in Figure 1C

claim: The Kolmogorov-Smirnov test suggested that males and females are not significantly different in their reward acquisition performance.
source: The KS test suggested that males and females are not just not significantly different in their reward acquisition performance (Kolmogorov-Smirnov D = 0.1875, p = 0.94), but that males and females have the same distributions for reward acquisition.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: Males and females have the same distributions for reward acquisition.
source: The KS test suggested that males and females are not just not significantly different in their reward acquisition performance (Kolmogorov-Smirnov D = 0.1875, p = 0.94), but that males and females have the same distributions for reward acquisition.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: Females responded significantly faster than did males.
source: Indeed, females responded significantly faster than did males (Figure 1C, main effect of sex, t (30) = 3.52, p = 0.0014), suggesting that decision making computations may differ across sexes and, if so, that the strategies that tended to be used by females resulted in faster choice response time than those used by males.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and shown in Figure 1D

claim: Decision making computations may differ across sexes.
source: Indeed, females responded significantly faster than did males (Figure 1C, main effect of sex, t (30) = 3.52, p = 0.0014), suggesting that decision making computations may differ across sexes and, if so, that the strategies that tended to be used by females resulted in faster choice response time than those used by males.
evidence: Inference from the observation of response time differences despite similar performance

claim: The strategies that tended to be used by females resulted in faster choice response time than those used by males.
source: Indeed, females responded significantly faster than did males (Figure 1C, main effect of sex, t (30) = 3.52, p = 0.0014), suggesting that decision making computations may differ across sexes and, if so, that the strategies that tended to be used by females resulted in faster choice response time than those used by males.
evidence: Inference from the observation of response time differences

claim: Prior research has shown that exploratory choices take longer than exploitative choices.
source: Prior research has shown that exploratory choices take longer than exploitative choices (Ebitz et al., 2019; Ebitz et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Males took longer to make a choice because a greater proportion of their choices were exploratory.
source: Therefore, perhaps males took longer to make a choice because a greater proportion of their choices were exploratory.
evidence: Hypothesis based on prior knowledge and observed response time differences

claim: In some previous studies, reinforcement learning (RL) models were used to quantify exploration via labeling choices that deviate from model values as exploratory.
source: In some previous studies, reinforcement learning (RL) models were used to quantify exploration (Cinotti et al., 2019; Daw et al., 2006; Ishii et al., 2002; Pearson et al., 2009) via labeling choices that deviate from model values as exploratory.
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: A non-reward maximizing goal would produce choices that are orthogonal to reward value, not errors of reward maximization.
source: However, a non-reward maximizing goal would produce choices that are orthogonal to reward value, not errors of reward maximization (Averbeck et al., 2017; Ebitz et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Recent studies have turned to an approach which models exploration as a latent state underlying behavior via a Hidden Markov model (HMM).
source: Therefore, recent studies have turned to an approach, which models exploration as a latent state underlying behavior via a Hidden Markov model (HMM), rather than inferring it from assumptions about values and learning (Ebitz et al., 2019; Ebitz et al., 2018; Muller et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: The HMM method has not previously been used to quantify exploration in mice.
source: The HMM method has not previously been used to quantify exploration in mice, so we first asked whether it was appropriate here.
evidence: Statement about the novelty of the approach in this context

claim: When agents exploit, they repeatedly sample the same option, switching only very rarely.
source: When agents exploit, they repeatedly sample the same option, switching only very rarely.
evidence: Based on established understanding of exploitation behavior

claim: Runs of exploratory choices tend not to repeat the same option and tend to switch far more frequently.
source: However, because exploration requires investigatory samples, runs of exploratory choices tend not to repeat the same option. They tend to switch far more frequently, closer to what we would expect from random samples from the environment (Ebitz et al., 2018).
evidence: Based on established understanding of exploration behavior and citation

claim: Choice run durations in mice were parsimoniously described as a mixture of two different patterns: one regime where choices switched quickly (mean switching time = 1.7 trials) and one regime where they changed slowly (mean switching time = 6.8 trials).
source: Indeed, choice run durations (i.e. the distribution of inter-switch intervals) were parsimoniously described as a mixture of two different patterns: one regime where choices switched quickly (mean switching time = 1.7 trials, compared to random choices at two trials; 80 % of choice runs) and one regime where they changed slowly (mean switching time = 6.8 trials; Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A

claim: Mice had evidence of fast-switching (putatively explore) and slow-switching (putatively exploit) regimes in their behavior.
source: Thus, mice had evidence of fast-switching (putatively explore) and slow-switching (putatively exploit) regimes in their behavior.
evidence: Inference from the mixture model analysis of choice run durations

claim: Response time was significantly longer during HMM-inferred exploration than exploitation.
source: The result suggested that response time was significantly longer during HMM-inferred exploration than exploitation (paired t-test, t(31) = 3.66, p = 0.0009), which is consistent with previous findings that exploration slows down decision making (Ebitz et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and consistent with prior literature

claim: Response time was significantly longer during RL-inferred exploration than exploitation.
source: Like HMM-inferred states, RL inferred explore-exploit states showed similar effects on response time - response time was significantly longer during exploration than exploitation (paired t-test, t(31) = 2.08, p = 0.046).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: The effect size of HMM labels on response time was over twice as big as that of RL labels.
source: However, the effect size of HMM labels on response time was over twice as big as that of RL labels (HMM: R2 = 0.30; RL: R2 = 0.12).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: The HMM-inferred states explained significantly more variance in response time than the RL-inferred states.
source: The result suggested that the HMM-inferred states explained significantly more variance in response time than the RL-inferred states in explaining response time.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C

claim: The two parameter HMM was the simplest, most interpretable, and best fit model.
source: The model comparisons have shown that the two parameter HMM was the simplest, most interpretable, and best fit model (AIC: 2 parameter HMM, AIC = 2976.1; ioHMM, AIC = 3117; ntHMM, AIC = 3101.5, see more statistics reported in Materials and methods).
evidence: Supported by model comparison statistics

claim: HMM-labeled exploratory choices were orthogonal to reward value.
source: Explore-labeled choices were non-reward-maximizing: they were orthogonal to reward value (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D; the average value of choices chosen during exploration was not different from chance; one sample t-test, t(10) = 0.16, p = 0.87).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D

claim: Reward learning was elevated during HMM-labeled exploratory states.
source: Reward learning was also elevated during exploration. During HMM-labeled exploratory states, the outcome of choices had more influence on the subsequent decision - animals were more likely to stay with the same choice if rewarded and switch if not rewarded (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F, two-way RM ANOVA, interaction term, F(1,31) = 51.2, p < 0.001).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2F

claim: There was no significant difference in reward retrieval time between exploratory and exploitative states.
source: There was no significant difference in reward retrieval time between two states (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G, t-test, t(31) = 0.05, p = 0.95), suggesting that animals were not more disengaged from the task during exploration than exploitation.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2G

claim: Animals were not more disengaged from the task during exploration than exploitation.
source: There was no significant difference in reward retrieval time between two states (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G, t-test, t(31) = 0.05, p = 0.95), suggesting that animals were not more disengaged from the task during exploration than exploitation.
evidence: Inference from the observation of no difference in reward retrieval time

claim: Males, on average, were more likely to be in the exploratory regime than the exploitative one, with 72.9% ± 11.5% STD of trials labeled as exploratory.
source: With more confidence in the validity of HMM-inferred states, we found that males, on average, were more likely to be in the exploratory regime than the exploitative one, with 72.9% ± 11.5% STD of trials labeled as exploratory (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and shown in Figure 1F

claim: Females explored much less with only 55.4% ± 20.4% STD of trials being exploratory.
source: Females explored much less with only 55.4% ± 20.4% STD of trials being exploratory (Figure 1F, t-test, t(30) = 2.98, p = 0.0056; 95% CI for the difference between the sexes = [5.5%, 29.3%]).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and shown in Figure 1F

claim: Males and females were reasonably, but not perfectly discriminable in terms of the proportion of exploratory choices (AUC = 0.76 ± 0.09).
source: As groups, males and females were reasonably, but not perfectly discriminable in terms of the proportion of exploratory choices (Figure 1G, receiver operating characteristic analysis, AUC = 0.76 ± 0.09, 95% CI for the difference = [0.59, 0.93], p = 0.013).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and shown in Figure 1G

claim: Males repeated exploration 92.1% (± 3.4% STD) of the time.
source: Males repeated exploration 92.1 % ( ± 3.4 % STD) of the time, while females stopped exploring and committed to a choice more quickly, repeating exploration only 83.1 % ( ± 16.8 % STD) of the time (t-test, t(30) = 2.09, P = 0.045, 95% CI for the difference = [0.2%, 17.8%]).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: Females stopped exploring and committed to a choice more quickly, repeating exploration only 83.1% (± 16.8% STD) of the time.
source: Males repeated exploration 92.1 % ( ± 3.4 % STD) of the time, while females stopped exploring and committed to a choice more quickly, repeating exploration only 83.1 % ( ± 16.8 % STD) of the time (t-test, t(30) = 2.09, P = 0.045, 95% CI for the difference = [0.2%, 17.8%]).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: There were no significant differences in the probability of repeating exploitation between males (83.5% ± 3.7%) and females (79.7 ± 22.1%).
source: There were no significant differences in the other parameter of the HMM (probability of repeating exploitation: males = 83.5% ± 3.7%; females = 79.7 ± 22.1 %; t(30) = 0.69, p = 0.5).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: Males were slower during both exploitation and exploration compared to females.
source: There was a significant main effect of state (main effect of state: F (1,30) = 13.07, p = 0.0011), but males were slower during females during both exploitation and exploration (main effect of sex, F(1,30) = 14.15, p = 0.0007) and there was no significant interaction (F (1,30) = 0.279, p = 0.60).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: In models fit to males, exploration was a deeper, more 'sticky' behavioral state (stationary probability of exploration = 68.0% ± 8.5% STD).
source: In models fit to males, exploration was a deeper, more 'sticky' behavioral state (Figure 1H, stationary probability of exploration = 68.0% ± 8.5% STD), compared to models fit to females, where exploration and exploitation were more closely matched (54.4% ± 18.4% STD; different from males: t(30) = 2.68, p = 0.012, 95% CI for the difference = [3.2%, 23.9%]).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of model dynamics and shown in Figure 1H

claim: In models fit to females, exploration and exploitation were more closely matched (stationary probability of exploration = 54.4% ± 18.4% STD).
source: In models fit to males, exploration was a deeper, more 'sticky' behavioral state (Figure 1H, stationary probability of exploration = 68.0% ± 8.5% STD), compared to models fit to females, where exploration and exploitation were more closely matched (54.4% ± 18.4% STD; different from males: t(30) = 2.68, p = 0.012, 95% CI for the difference = [3.2%, 23.9%]).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of model dynamics and shown in Figure 1H

claim: Males were more likely to get 'stuck' in an extended exploratory period, requiring more energy to escape from exploring and start exploiting a good choice.
source: This suggests that males were more likely to get 'stuck' in an extended exploratory period, requiring more energy to escape from exploring and start exploiting a good choice.
evidence: Inference from the analysis of model dynamics showing deeper exploratory states in males

claim: Both the learning rate parameter (α) and the decision-noise parameter (inverse temperature β) can influence exploration in RL models.
source: However, exploration in an RL model should be a function of both the difference in subjective values and the decision-noise in the model. This is because both parameters increase the likelihood that agents will make non-reward-maximizing decisions (Figure 2A).
evidence: Demonstrated through simulation and shown in Figure 2

claim: Changing the decision-noise parameter (β) robustly changed the probability of exploration in simulated RL agents.
source: As expected, changing the decision-noise parameter (β) robustly changed the probability of exploration (Figure 2B; GLM, main effect of inverse temperature, β1 = –0.11, p < 0.0001): the larger the inverse temperature, the lower the decision noise and the lower probability of exploration.
evidence: Supported by simulation data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2B

claim: Learning rate (α) influenced the probability of exploration in simulated RL agents.
source: Critically, learning rate (ɑ) also influenced the probability of exploration (Figure 2B; GLM, main effect of learning rate, β2 = –0.10, p < 0.0001).
evidence: Supported by simulation data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2B

claim: Learning rate (α) and decision noise (β) interacted to influence exploration in simulated RL agents.
source: In fact, there were some values for learning rate (ɑ) at which changing decision noise had no effect on exploration whatsoever: ɑ and β interacted to influence exploration (Figure 2C; GLM, interaction term, β3 = –0.38, p < 0.0001).
evidence: Supported by simulation data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2C

claim: When the learning rate was very low, agents failed to move away from the high-decision-noise regime at all, meaning that there was little effect of any additional noise.
source: This occurred because when the learning rate was very low, agents failed to move away from the high-decision-noise regime at all, meaning that there was little effect of any additional noise.
evidence: Inference from simulation results

claim: The four-parameter RLCK model had the highest relative likelihood in both sexes among seven reinforcement learning models tested.
source: Although model fitting was slightly different across sexes, in both males and females, the "RLCK" model, four-parameter model with value and choice kernel updating policies, best characterized animals' choice behaviors in this task among all seven models (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by model comparison statistics shown in Figure 3B

claim: The RL models with parameter(s) that account for choice bias (RLCK, RLCKγ, RLCKη) were significantly better at predicting animals' actual choices than the models that do not account for choice bias and non-RL models.
source: The results suggested that the RL models with parameter(s) that account for choice bias (RLCK, RLCKγ, RLCKη) were significantly better at predicting animals' actual choices than the models that do not account for choice bias and non-RL models (random, noisy WSLS, RL, RLε).
evidence: Supported by model agreement analysis

claim: Females had significantly higher learning rate (α) than males.
source: We found that females had significantly higher learning rate (α) than males (Figure 3D, t(30) = 2.40, p = 0.02) but there was no significant difference across sexes in other parameters (β: t(30) = 1.44, p = 0.16; αc: t(30) = 1.40, P = 0.17; βc: t(30) = 1.73, p = 0.09).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of model parameters and shown in Figure 3D

claim: There was no significant difference across sexes in inverse temperature (β), choice bias (αc), or choice stickiness (βc) parameters.
source: We found that females had significantly higher learning rate (α) than males (Figure 3D, t(30) = 2.40, p = 0.02) but there was no significant difference across sexes in other parameters (β: t(30) = 1.44, p = 0.16; αc: t(30) = 1.40, P = 0.17; βc: t(30) = 1.73, p = 0.09).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of model parameters

claim: Males and females were reasonably discriminable in terms of the learning rate (AUC = 0.72 ± 0.09).
source: As groups, males and females were reasonably discriminable in terms of the learning rate (Figure 3E, receiver operating characteristic analysis, AUC = 0.72 ± 0.09, 95% CI for the difference = [0.54, 0.90], p = 0.035).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 3E

claim: The difference in the level of exploration between males and females was not due to differences in decision noise, but instead due to differences in learning rate.
source: These results suggested that the difference in the level of exploration between males and females was not due to differences in decision noise, but instead due to differences in learning rate.
evidence: Inference from the RL model parameter analysis

claim: The learning rate parameter in an RL model does not equate to the learning performance.
source: While females had significantly higher learning rate (α) than males, they did not obtain more rewards than males. This is because the learning rate parameter in an RL model does not equate to the learning performance, which is better measured by the number of rewards obtained.
evidence: Based on understanding of RL model parameters

claim: A higher learning rate in a RL model does not translate to better reward acquisition performance.
source: A higher learning rate in a RL model does not translate to better reward acquisition performance.
evidence: Demonstrated through simulation shown in Figure 3F

claim: Different combinations of learning rate and decision noise can result in the same reward acquisition performance.
source: To illustrate that different combinations of learning rate and decision noise can result in the same reward acquisition performance. We conducted computer simulations of 10,000 RL agents defined by different combinations of learning rate (ɑ) and inverse temperature (β-1) and plotted their reward acquisition performance for the restless bandit task (Figure 3F, temperature instead of inverse temperature was plotted for the ease of presentation).
evidence: Demonstrated through simulation shown in Figure 3F

claim: The optimal reward acquisition is achieved when learning rate is moderate.
source: This figure demonstrates that (1) different learning rate and inverse temperature combinations can result in similar performance, (2) the optimal reward acquisition is achieved when learning rate is moderate.
evidence: Demonstrated through simulation shown in Figure 3F

claim: Females, but not males, showed increased learning rate over experience with task.
source: One interesting finding is that, when compared learning rate across sessions within sex, females, but not males, showed increased learning rate over experience with task (Figure 3G, repeated measures ANOVA, female: main effect of time, F (2.26,33.97) = 5.27, p = 0.008; male: main effect of time, F(2.5,37.52) = 0.23, p = 0.84).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 3G

claim: The increased learning rate over sessions in females points to potential sex differences in meta-learning.
source: This points to potential sex differences in meta-learning that could contribute to the differential strategies across sexes.
evidence: Inference from the observation of learning rate changes over time

claim: Animals tended to repeat the previous choice after obtaining a reward.
source: The results revealed an expected significant main effect of outcome on stay-switch decisions (main effect of outcome, p < 0.00001). This effect was driven by the tendency of animals to repeat the previous choice (i.e.: not switching) after obtaining a reward (post hoc t-test compared to chance at 0.50, mean = 0.75, 95% CI = [0.74, 0.77], t(255)=34.33, p < 0.0001) and a much smaller tendency to switch more often than chance after reward omission (mean = 0.52, 95% CI = [0.50, 0.55], post hoc t-test, t(255) = 2.05, p = 0.04).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: Females were more likely to repeat a previous choice and males were more likely to switch.
source: The tendency to switch or stay also differed by sex, with females more likely to repeat a previous choice and males more likely to switch (main effect of sex, p < 0.00001; post-hoc t-test on p(switch): t(254) = 4.12, p < 0.0001).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: There was a significant interaction effect between sex and outcome on stay-switch decisions.
source: There was also a significant interaction effect between sex and outcome (sex X reward interaction, p < 0.00001).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: Female mice displayed more win-stay behaviors than males.
source: We found that female mice displayed more win-stay behaviors, indicating that they were more likely than the males to repeat behaviors that produced reward on the previous trial (Figure 4A, sex X reward interaction, p < 0.000001, Supplementary file 1; post hoc t-test: t(254) = 5.53, p < 0.0001).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and shown in Figure 4A

claim: Males and females were reasonably, but not perfectly discriminable in terms of the proportion of win stay choices (AUC = 0.74 ± 0.09).
source: As groups, males and females were reasonably, but not perfectly discriminable in terms of the proportion of win stay choices (Figure 4B, receiver operating characteristic analysis, AUC = 0.74 ± 0.09, 95% CI for the difference = [0.56, 0.92], p = 0.0195).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 4B

claim: Male mice tended to shift even when the previous choice was rewarded.
source: In contrast, male mice tended to shift even when the previous choice was rewarded.
evidence: Inference from the observation of lower win-stay behavior in males

claim: There was no significant sex difference in learning from losses (lose-shift behavior).
source: There was no significant sex difference in learning from losses (Figure 4C and t(25) = 1.40, p = 0.16), but this did not mean that sex differences in learning were solely due to sex differences in learning from wins.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and shown in Figure 4C

claim: Males switched less after losses than females within exploratory states.
source: Males switched less after losses than females within exploratory states (Figure 4D; post hoc t-test on session averages: sex difference within exploration: p < 0.001, t(251) = 3.39), though there was no significant sex difference within exploitation (p = 0.06, t(243) = 1.87; note that differing degrees of freedom are due to the fact that exploitation was not observed in some sessions for some animals).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and shown in Figure 4D

claim: There was no significant sex difference in lose-shift behavior within exploitation.
source: Males switched less after losses than females within exploratory states (Figure 4D; post hoc t-test on session averages: sex difference within exploration: p < 0.001, t(251) = 3.39), though there was no significant sex difference within exploitation (p = 0.06, t(243) = 1.87; note that differing degrees of freedom are due to the fact that exploitation was not observed in some sessions for some animals).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: The increased tendency to win-stay in females was driven by the explore choices.
source: We also found that the increased tendency to win-stay that we observed in females was driven by the explore choices (Figure 4E; post-hoc t-test: p = 0.015, t(251) = 2.55).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and shown in Figure 4E

claim: There was no significant difference in win-stay between males and females during exploit choices.
source: There was no significant difference in win-stay between males and females during exploit choices (post-hoc t-test: p = 0.09, t(244) = 1.68).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: Females were better explorers (i.e.: they had increased reward learning during exploration), whereas males learned slower during exploration but compensated for this learning disadvantage by exploring more frequently.
source: Together these results suggest that females were better explorers (i.e.: they had increased reward learning during exploration), whereas males learned slower during exploration but compensated for this learning disadvantage by exploring more frequently.
evidence: Inference from the combined observations of learning differences during exploration

claim: There was a significant three-way interaction between sex, explore/exploit state, and reward on stay-switch decisions.
source: Critically, there was also a significant three-way interaction between sex, explore/exploit state, and reward (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 1, sex X reward X state interaction, p = 0.0438).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and shown in Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: Mutual information was higher in females than males.
source: The result suggested that mutual information was higher in females than males, suggesting that females were using more information from the past choice and outcome to make their current decision. (Figure 4G, t(30) = 2.65, p = 0.013).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and shown in Figure 4G

claim: Females were using more information from the past choice and outcome to make their current decision.
source: The result suggested that mutual information was higher in females than males, suggesting that females were using more information from the past choice and outcome to make their current decision. (Figure 4G, t(30) = 2.65, p = 0.013).
evidence: Inference from the observation of higher mutual information in females

claim: Males and females were reasonably discriminable in terms of mutual information (AUC = 0.74 ± 0.09).
source: As groups, males and females were reasonably discriminable in terms of mutual information (Figure 4H, receiver operating characteristic analysis, AUC = 0.74 ± 0.09, 95% CI for the difference = [0.57, 0.92], p = 0.0195).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 4H

claim: Males learned less during exploration and as a result, they had to explore for longer to learn which option was worth exploiting.
source: Our major finding that males learned less during exploration and explored for longer is consistent with two explanations. First, males learned more slowly during exploration and as a result, they had to explore for longer to learn which option was worth exploiting.
evidence: Inference from experimental observations

claim: Males got 'stuck' in extended periods of exploration that prohibited them from applying the knowledge they have learned and committing to a rewarding option.
source: Another possibility is that males got 'stuck' in extended periods of exploration that prohibited them from applying the knowledge they have learned and committing to a rewarding option.
evidence: Inference from experimental observations

claim: The HMM model was able to label a meaningful exploratory state that matches normative definitions of exploration in the mouse model.
source: In our data, we have shown for the first time that the HMM model was able to label a meaningful exploratory state that matches normative definitions of exploration in the mouse model.
evidence: Supported by validation analyses of HMM-inferred states

claim: Differences in exploration between the sexes were due to differences in learning rates, not due to differences in the decision noise parameter.
source: However, our findings indicate that multiple latent parameters can influence how much these models explore. Here, we found that differences in exploration between the sexes were due to differences in learning rates, not due to differences in the decision noise parameter, which is more commonly associated with exploration.
evidence: Supported by RL model parameter analysis

claim: Dopamine is implicated in reinforcement learning, including the transition between exploration and exploitation, and is strongly sex-modulated.
source: One neuromodulator that is implicated in reinforcement learning, including the transition between exploration and exploitation, and is strongly sex-modulated is dopamine (Beeler et al., 2010; Jenni et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Dopamine signals regulate exploration via mechanisms of action selection and learning.
source: Studies have shown that dopamine signals regulate exploration via mechanisms of action selection and learning (Beeler et al., 2010; Frank et al., 2009; Humphries et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Estradiol has been demonstrated to exert both acute and chronic modulatory effects on dopamine release, reuptake, and receptor binding.
source: For example, estradiol has been demonstrated to exert both acute and chronic modulatory effects on dopamine release, reuptake, and receptor binding (Yoest et al., 2014), allowing enhanced DA release and faster DA clearance in females (Becker, 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Estradiol allows enhanced DA release and faster DA clearance in females.
source: For example, estradiol has been demonstrated to exert both acute and chronic modulatory effects on dopamine release, reuptake, and receptor binding (Yoest et al., 2014), allowing enhanced DA release and faster DA clearance in females (Becker, 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: The mechanism of enhanced DA release and faster DA clearance in females could contribute to increased reward learning observed in females during exploration.
source: This mechanism could contribute to increased reward learning observed in females during exploration.
evidence: Speculative inference connecting known dopamine mechanisms to observed behavioral differences

claim: The prefrontal cortex (PFC) is a target brain region to understand exploration and exploitation.
source: The prefrontal cortex (PFC), which receives dopamine projections, is a target brain region to understand exploration and exploitation (Ebitz et al., 2018; Jenni et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: A previous study by the authors implicated PFC in the differences in learning strategy between males and females.
source: Our previous study implicated PFC in the differences in learning strategy between males and females (Chen et al., 2021b).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work by the authors

claim: Prefrontal cortical dopamine may be particularly engaged in implementing explore-exploit strategies via sex-biased mechanisms of learning.
source: It is possible that prefrontal cortical dopamine is particularly engaged in implementing explore-exploit strategies via sex-biased mechanisms of learning.
evidence: Speculative inference about neural mechanisms

claim: There is an emerging trend among rodent researchers with adopting tasks with translational potentials in rodents, such as reversal learning and various versions of bandit task.
source: Currently, there is an emerging exciting trend among rodent researchers with adopting tasks with translational potentials in rodents, such as reversal learning and various versions of bandit task (Izquierdo et al., 2019; Groman et al., 2016; Bari et al., 2019; Grossman et al., 2021), where we can assess the same cognitive processes across species and across animal models of diseases.
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Explore-exploit decisions are shared cognitive processes across species.
source: Here, we establish that explore-exploit decisions are shared cognitive processes across species, making this restless bandit task an ideal tool for translational research.
evidence: Inference from the successful application of the task in mice and its use in other species

claim: Parallel approaches in humans have been used to examine the explore-exploit strategic phenotype of neuropsychiatric disorders, including ADHD, addiction, and depression.
source: Parallel approaches in humans have been used to examine the explore-exploit strategic phenotype of neuropsychiatric disorders, including ADHD, addiction, and depression (Addicott et al., 2021; Addicott et al., 2012; Beeler et al., 2012; Blanco et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Thirty-two BL6129SF1/J mice (16 males and 16 females) were obtained from Jackson Laboratories.
source: Thirty-two BL6129SF1/J mice (16 males and 16 females) were obtained from Jackson Laboratories (stock #101043).
evidence: Direct description of experimental methods

claim: Mice arrived at the lab at 7 weeks of age.
source: Mice arrived at the lab at 7 weeks of age, and they were housed in groups of four with ad libitum access to water while being mildly food restricted (85–95% of free feeding weight) for the experiment.
evidence: Direct description of experimental methods

claim: Animals engaging in operant testing were housed in a 0900–2100 hours reversed light cycle to permit testing during the dark period.
source: Animals engaging in operant testing were housed in a 0900–2100 hours reversed light cycle to permit testing during the dark period.
evidence: Direct description of experimental methods

claim: On average across all sessions, animals performed 276.5 trials with a standard deviation of 8.6 trials.
source: On average across all sessions, animals performed 276.5 trials with a standard deviation of 8.6 trials (male average: 253.7 trials, sd = 15.4; female average 299.3 trials, sd = 0.74).
evidence: Direct description of experimental data

claim: Choice run durations (inter-switch intervals) will be exponentially distributed if choice runs end probabilistically.
source: To the extent that choice runs end probabilistically (an assumption of the HMM framework), choice run durations (inter-switch intervals) will be exponentially distributed (Berg, 1993).
evidence: Based on established statistical theory and citation

claim: Adding a second mixing distribution significantly improved model fit for inter-switch intervals.
source: Adding a second mixing distribution significantly improved model fit (one-component, one-parameter mixture log-likelihood: –44555, two-component, three-parameter: –41656; likelihood ratio test, p < 10–32).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of model fit

claim: A mixture of one fast-switching regime and one slow-switching regime was the most parsimonious explanation for the inter-switch interval data.
source: This suggests that a mixture of one fast-switching regime and one slow-switching regime was the most parsimonious explanation for the data (McLachlan and Peel, 2004).
evidence: Inference from model comparison analysis and citation

claim: The HMM had only two free parameters: one corresponding to the probability of exploring given exploration on the last trial, and one corresponding to the probability of exploiting given exploitation on the last trial.
source: Through fixing the emissions model, constraining the structure of the transmission matrix, and tying the parameters, the final HMM had only two free parameters: one corresponding to the probability of exploring, given exploration on the last trial, and one corresponding to the probability of exploiting, given exploitation on the last trial.
evidence: Direct description of model structure

claim: The model was fit via expectation-maximization using the Baum Welch algorithm.
source: The model was fit via expectation-maximization using the Baum Welch algorithm (Bilmes, 1998).
evidence: Direct description of methods with citation

claim: The input-output HMM model (ioHMM) improved model fit compared to the two-parameter original HMM.
source: The ioHMM model improved model fit (two-parameter original HMM: log-likelihood = –1424.0; 4-parameter ioHMM: log-likelihood = –1430.5).
evidence: Supported by model comparison statistics

claim: The AIC test suggested that the original two-parameter HMM was the better model compared to the four-parameter ioHMM.
source: The result of model comparison using both AIC suggested that the original two-parameter model was the better model (AIC: two-parameter original HMM: AIC = 2976.1; four-parameter ioHMM: AIC = 3117; relative likelihood (AIC weight) of the four-parameter ioHMM <10^–30).
evidence: Supported by model comparison statistics
